questions.q: A user checks out with three different catalog items in one cart. How many records does ServiceNow create?
options: Three sc_request records, one per item
One single record covering the whole order with no line-item breakdown
One sc_request record and three sc_req_item records, one per item
One sc_req_item record shared by all three items
questions.explain: One sc_request represents the overall order; each catalog item ordered gets its own sc_req_item record.

questions.q: What field ties a Requested Item back to its parent Request?
options: The `request` reference field on sc_req_item, pointing at the sc_request record
A free-text field where the requester types the request number
There is no structural link — the two tables are unrelated
A Data Policy that matches records by submission date
questions.explain: sc_req_item.request is the reference field every rollup and related list relies on to connect the two tables.

questions.q: A request contains three Requested Items: two are Closed Complete, one is still Work in Progress. What should the Request's own rollup state show?
options: Closed Complete, because most of the items are done
The Request has no state of its own, only the items do
Work in Progress is irrelevant once any item is closed
A status reflecting that it is not fully done yet, such as Partially Complete, calculated from the items underneath it
questions.explain: Closing the Request before every item is done would falsely tell the requester the whole order is finished.

questions.q: Why does an SLA commitment for fulfilling a request usually attach to the Requested Item rather than the overall Request?
options: SLAs cannot technically be attached to sc_request at all
Different items in the same order can have different fulfillment paths and different SLA commitments, so each item needs its own due date and breach condition
The Request table does not support any time-based fields
Attaching SLAs to the Request is always the correct and only approach
questions.explain: A single checkout can mix items with very different fulfillment realities — the SLA needs to match each item, not the order as a whole.

questions.q: Why does Request Management use a two-table model (sc_request plus sc_req_item) instead of one flat record per order?
options: Because fulfillment happens item by item, often by different teams, and each item needs its own state and assignment group without being tangled up with other items in the same order
It is a legacy limitation with no real implementation benefit
Flat records are technically impossible to build in ServiceNow
The split exists only to make reporting harder on purpose
questions.explain: A laptop, a monitor, and a software license in one cart may need three different fulfillers — the item-level split keeps each one's work isolated and trackable.
